utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin and Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too. You may sit down, too, thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, also Denise Gustin, who is temporarily absent from court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I appear with Milka Maglov co-counsel and Tania Radosavljevic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Appearances for General Talic? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] I am Xavier de Roux attorney assisted by my co-counsel, Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, and Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci and good morning. Thank you. I think we can proceed. Yes, Ms. Korner? I thought we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can in fact, Your Honour, but may I just raise two administrative matters before the witness comes in? Your Honour it's very difficult to estimate, as Your Honour has seen, witness's length, but in theory we may have two days in the week before we break for Easter left where witnesses will be finished. Your Honour, I am reluctant to bring witnesses relating to the Sanski Most municipality just before Easter, in case we don't get there, and what I was hoping to suggest, with the concurrence of Defence counsel is that if there is any time left over, it seems to me that one of the exercises that will have to be done is that we go through the documents in the Banja Luka binders which have not at the moment been specifically referred to by any witnesses so that an at least Your Honours have seen what's in there. Later on other witnesses will be dealing with them, but it's very difficult to estimate when, and if one wants to look at a municipality as a whole, it seems to me that's an exercise however tedious that will have to be gone through. And, therefore, I would ask if there is time available, we do it at that stage rather than getting Sanski Most witnesses. Your, Honour that's the first matter. The second matter is in relation to the matter we discussed yesterday, that of the journalist. Both myself and Mr. Ackerman independently have had an opportunity to speak to the journalist who actually did the interpreting. For the moment, can I say this to Your Honour: We are still in discussions about what's going to happen. There is still, however, the matter outstanding of the witness summons that was issued for Mr. Randall and which is returnable on Monday or potentially Wednesday. I would simply ask Your Honours to say for the moment that that witness summons can, as it were, remain in abeyance until we have had a further chance to see whether we can sort this matter out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I really have nothing to add to what Ms. Korner said about that, about either of those things. I do have another separate matter. There is a document which I have marked DB46A and 46B, Your Honours. It -- you won't have it. It is in reference to the Prosecutor's Exhibit 25A and B, which is the Variant A/B document that was the subject of discussion earlier in the case. This document was apparently handed to me by the Prosecutor after we had had the discussions regarding the Variant A/B document and I didn't discover that that had happened until yesterday so I'm bringing it to you at the first opportunity. I think I want to just offer it into evidence for whatever light it may throw and assist with regard to both the authenticity and the weight of that Variant A/B document. I will tell you just very briefly that as I understand it, this is a letter that was generated as a result of an inquiry from the Office of the Prosecutor regarding that particular document, which is 25, and the reply from the SDS is that they have -- that investigation has been carried out apparently, and that there never was any document instructing the organisation and activation of the Serb people of BiH that came from the SDS. They say they were informed that those instructions were given by retired officers of the former JNA, which I don't know what that means, but in any event I'd like to offer this as an exhibit for whatever it might be worth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour may recall that we never actually had the discussion about variant or the submissions because the Defence withdrew their objections. Now, I'm entirely -- Mr. Ackerman is incorrect. At the time when we gave the documents in respect of this discussion to the Defence, I was wholly unaware that the particular letter existed. It's no excuse. It's simply, as Your Honour may appreciate, there are a number of teams working in this office and occasionally communication does break down. However, if it is now to be suggested that there is still going to be a submission that the Variant A and B document is not authentic, was not issued, as we suggest, by the SDS, then we will have to reopen the whole matter because it's an important matter. As I say, we were unaware of this letter. We do not accept -- may I say, a request was sent to the Republika Srpska asking for the distribution list of the document, and what we received was this letter saying nothing to do with them. We do not accept that for one moment. And Your Honour, there is ample evidence we will be suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was not expecting you to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I put it this way? It came as somewhat of a surprise to me that the letter had in fact been written given we were aware that the SDS was very unhappy about that this document. So but nonetheless we say that there is ample other evidence which we would wish to call before Your Honour to show that this is a genuine document so therefore, I have no objections to Mr. Ackerman putting it in, but if the suggestion is still from the Defence that this is not an authentic document, then I would wish to reopen the argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's close this parenthesis on this particular document. Do you have anything else to add in regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just very briefly. Ms. Korner just told us that she was aware that the SDS was very unhappy about this document. I wonder if there is additional correspondence that bears on this matter that would support that, that we should also be given. I mean do they have a letter from the SDS saying they are very unhappy about this document or anything of that nature? I haven't -- that hasn't been part of the evidence in the case. And I think it's important that we know where that comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Maitre de Roux? Anything you may have to say with regard to the point -- two points raised by Ms. Korner and the point raised by Mr. Ackerman? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add to what has been said by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Maitre de Roux. So I take it the position is as follows: You are exhibiting this particular document, Mr. Ackerman, as D46 -- DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: DB46A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: DB46A and B, so that's number one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, the question hasn't been answered. Is it still disputed by the Defence that this is not an authentic document that was issued by the main board of the SDS on or about the 19th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it is redisputed at this point, Your Honour. I think this sheds light on the issue and I understand that the issue is still being debated in the Bosanski Samac case and all I can tell you is that what I've heard is that that Trial Chamber has some concern about the effect of this particular bit of correspondence so I think the matter does have to be raised again. I'm not sure it has to be raised now, but I think at some point in this trial I will ask you to reconsider the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood you anyway. So if I were you, Ms. Korner, assume that to an extent at least it is being reopened. Remembering also, Mr. Ackerman, that when you at a certain point in time withdrew your objection regarding that or the authenticity of that document, you withdrew it because of the signatures and written words, handwritten words, that there were on the document that was exhibited. I remember you discussing it with your colleague and it was after you noticed that there were some handwritten notes and some signatures on that document that you accepted the authenticity. However, I do concede that given the existence of this new document, which sheds a certain -- casts a certain measure of possible doubt, we will have the matter reopened at whichever point you choose. I will leave it up to you. Provided you exchange information beforehand so that one doesn't surprise the other. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In other words, if you intend to reopen it at any given time please tell Ms. Korner or Mr. Cayley or whoever will be in charge of that particular part so that they will be prepared with the necessary evidence, if necessary. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will find a convenient time to deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So -- and with regard to any possible examination or review of the remaining documents in the Banja Luka files, which could be done the last two days before we stop for our Easter break, would you live with that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I -- well, yeah. My intention, Your Honour, is to depart The Hague on the 22nd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was my intention, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the morning because the flight on the 22nd is very late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm leaving in the morning, about 10.40 in the morning, I think. If you're sitting here reading documents, I don't think it would be totally necessary that I sit here and listen to that so I might ask your permission to depart if Ms. Korner is going to be reading documents to you. I fail to see that there is much value in her reading you the documents since I think you're totally capable of reading them yourselves but that's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you didn't mean or intend to stay or expect us three to stay listening to you while you read all those documents. I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- I tell you -- first of all, we are not sitting the 22nd because it's a court maintenance day so we stop on the 21st. Your Honour, I was. I appreciate it, of course, is different when one is dealing with professional judges rather than a jury, but nonetheless, the temptation when one has binders of documents is that one reads very quickly, but if Your Honours would prefer simply to sit and read through the documents yourselves, then I'm quite content. It's merely an exercise to get us all to look at the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In my jurisdiction, Ms. Korner, usually when a lawyer stands up and starts reading either from previous case law or from an author or a book or whatever, we just ask for the reference and we always say, "The Court knows how to read." Any way, I personally -- I think -- let's give us time to discuss it so that I discuss it with the other two judges and then we come back to you, because this is something that I have not discussed as yet. I mean, I personally -- my preference would be to prefer you to indicate which of those documents you are relying more than others. I think it's more important for us to sift the wheat from the chaff and rather than have to read all the documents if you yourself believe that some are more important than others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have done a major sifting exercise already, but I leave it to Your Honours to decide and then if Your Honours decide that you would prefer to simply have a list, as it were, of documents, and read them yourselves, then of course, we will comply, but effectively our view would be that we've already selected from the hundreds of thousands of documents the ones that we do think are important and they are in these binders. However, we'll leave it with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will come back to you on this. Yes, Maitre de Roux? I see you on edge. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that if we need to read the documents that are already in the record, this is of little interest, because each of us can read them. If on the other hand, the Prosecution believes that some of the documents present difficulties of interpretation and the Prosecution has a certain interpretation of certain documents, then we need to discuss it. But if it is simply taking into consideration, becoming familiarised with documents and reading those documents, I think that is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will discuss it amongst ourselves and then we will tell you later what we think, because it may well be that there may be some documents which would you like to furnish explanations or not just read but -- I don't know. We will discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can call in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usher will give you once more the same document you saw yesterday, containing the statement that you read out, and you are kindly asked to read it out, to make that statement again in court this morning before you proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you may continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, we were talking yesterday about your committee which was dealing with effectively people who were detained and whether or not the Geneva Conventions were being complied with. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Translate in French, maybe. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Interpreters, please, apparently the witness is receiving interpretation in French.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was the button, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It was the button. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question or has it being translated into English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In B/C/S, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in the Bosnia language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was in French. I was getting the interpretation into French, but now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you may proceed and I would suggest that you put the question again, please, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't really a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, this morning I want to take up where we left off yesterday, namely your attempts to visit camps. You told us that you were unable to arrange a visit to any of the camps in Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a camp named Manjaca. Were you able to visit that camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to visit the Manjaca camp and we actually visited it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you how you were able to make arrangements. When did you first hear about Manjaca, roughly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the Manjaca camp roughly towards the end of the month of April, 1992. But anyway, I know that in Manjaca, there is a military exercise area. Earlier on, while the former JNA existed, and even I myself as a student, spent 15 days in that military training grounds for exercises, military training, and towards the end of April, 1992, we learnt that there was a military camp at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that you were able to arrange to visit the camp. Who did you first speak to about going to the camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- or rather I, Mr. Adil Medic, Professor Bajric, and Imam Alija Halilovic, we went to the former building of the Yugoslav People's Army, that is the military command in the town of Banja Luka, where the 1st Krajina Corps was headquartered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause there for a moment. You say the former JNA building. By the time you visited that building, had it become the 1st Krajina Corps, the Banja Luka Corps, or was it still the 5th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two buildings there. One was called the JNA Club, and next to it was another building where the command was. I know that a part of the Yugoslav People's Army was still there because roughly about that time, the Serb authorities in Banja Luka started setting up certain judicial military institutions such as the attorney, the military prosecutor's office, the military courts, and there were officers of the Yugoslav People's Army and the command of the Krajina Corps of the Banja Luka Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that was -- I think you misunderstood slightly. I didn't want to interrupt you, Mr. Dzonlic. By the time you paid a visit, had the 5th Corps of the JNA, which was the Banja Luka Corps, been transferred to the Bosnian Serb Army, the VRS, and was now called the 1st Corps? In other words, had the change taken place?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the transformation had taken place because they said then that it was the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you went to the building with the people that you've mentioned. Had you made an appointment in advance?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't make an appointment in advance. We just there went directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to speak on that first occasion to any senior officer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that first occasion, when we arrived, we just registered with the porter, the porter's office, which was to the left of the entrance to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the officer on duty. We said we were from Merhamet, we introduced ourselves and said that we would like to see the corps commander. He asked us what about and we said in connection with the Manjaca camp. However, on that occasion, we were unable to see the commander or his deputies or heads of departments. We were told to come back a couple of days later. So we went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you went back, do you know who you spoke to, the name of the officer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, a name that was mentioned was Stevilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what position Stevilovic held within the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was head of security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, on that second occasion, was there anybody with him or was he on his own, that is Stevilovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say with precision, whether this was the second time that we went there or maybe the third, because we went there several times on a number of occasions, the four -- sometimes the four of us, sometimes the three of us or two of us, requesting to talk to somebody in a position of responsibility, whether this was the second, the third or fourth time, I cannot tell you. But on one of those instances, when we arrived, he introduced himself as Stevilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you seek the assistance of anybody outside the military to arrange to speak to a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we found out about the existence of the camp in Manjaca, we did seek for someone. I personally went to the International Red Cross to see Mr. Beat who was responsible for Banja Luka municipality and I informed him of my information on the existence of the camp. I told him that as the International Red Cross, they were responsible to act on the basis of the information to take certain measures which were in accordance with their responsibilities and to go to the military command and, if possible, to make this possible for us too, to go there. And I think that I also went to see representatives of the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other than international organisations, did you speak to anybody in authority in Banja Luka itself?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We also went to the president of the municipality of Banja Luka, Mr. Predrag Radic, and we also informed him of these facts and he said that we should go to that command, since it was a military command, and we had to contact the command directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us that Mr. Brdjanin was the president of the ARK Crisis Staff. Did you approach him or seek to approach him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any reason why you didn't seek to approach him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't really provide any clarifications on this matter. We didn't go to see him because we found out that that was a matter of military authority, it was under the army, and for this reason we went to the military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did there come a time after however many visits it was, where you were able to speak to a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, we managed to enter the building of the command, we were met by an officer. I think his name was Stevilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. You told us about a meeting with Mr. Stevilovic. Were you able to meet with anyone more senior than him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, General Talic was also present, and he said that his chief of security, Stevilovic, a dark officer was by his side, and a grey man with glasses was there too. I later recognised him as a commander of the camp. He said that they were responsible for the camp and that with regard to the camp, we would solve all issues with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did General Talic tell you anything about Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only said that it was a military camp and that with regard to the camp, we would address matters with the -- we would solve the issues with his officers who were responsible for the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He told you it was a military camp. Did he tell you under which arm of the military this camp came? In other words, which particular corps?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Another officer said that it was a military camp under the 1st Krajina Corps and that all the prisoners, all the detainees, were prisoners of war and that they were being treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When that other officer told you that, was General Talic present?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How long was -- roughly how long a conversation did you have with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was short. He only came and he said -- well, maybe it was three to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To whom did you explain why you had come to the corps command, in full?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We explained this to the officers. I think that the commander of the camp was present, his name was Popovic. The officer for security was there, who said that his name was Stevilovic. A dark officer was there. They called him "captain."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you tell these officers that you wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We told them that we had heard about the existence of this camp and we said that we wanted to help people in the camp, and that we wanted to give them food and medicine because we had heard that there were quite a few sick people and that they didn't have enough food and that if it was possible that they should authorise us to visit this camp and to send them food, medicine, clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Popovic or any of the other officers tell you anything about the conditions in the camp when you explained what you wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were very decisive. As I said earlier on, they said that, "This was a camp under the 1st Krajina Corps, that the prisoners were prisoners of war, and that they were being treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." They also said that there were sick people there and that they didn't have enough food.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they give you an explanation, any sort of explanation, as to why the prisoners were not getting enough food?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just said that they didn't have enough food.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, was it agreed at that meeting that you could visit the camp or did that come at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't told that we would be authorised to enter the camp then, but they said that we should come again in a few days' time and that they would consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so did you return?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned twice perhaps after that, and I was interested in finding out whether we had received authorisation, but we didn't receive an answer, and I think that at the time some other person was communicating with us. He introduced himself as Bogilovic. He was there instead of Mr. Stevilovic. He said he was the one responsible for contact with us. On two or three occasions I went to the command, perhaps every other day or every third day. However, after a certain time, I can't remember exactly whether it was ten days or 20 days, Mr. Adil Medic came to our office and he said that we had been authorised to visit the Manjaca camp and that we should prepare our papers, copies of our identity cards, in order to have them obtain a permission to enter and we had to specify the time and the day of departure, when we would go to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just before we come to Manjaca itself, your visit, can you remember, did you meet at any stage, any other officers whose name you can remember in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, I can't remember. I met quite a few people there, quite a few officers, but I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that you spoke to an officer about visiting -- I'm sorry, I'm not sure you did. Did you ever speak to a military officer about visiting the Prijedor camps?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we deal with the visit, please, that you made to Manjaca? I don't think there is any dispute about these matters, who you went with. You went there, I think, with the Imam Halilovic, Professor Bajric and Mr. Medic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The four of us went there and I have just remembered this name, another man went with us, Makic, Ibrahim went with us. He provided his red Kombi, he had a red Kombi, and we went there in this red Kombi, and the four of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think you were escorted to the camp by two military jeeps; is that right? In fact, three in all?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were two military jeeps in front of us. And there was another military vehicle behind us as an escort and we went to that command, from that command maybe at about 9.00 in the morning, 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the camp, did you see that there was a fence surrounding it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that the camp was entirely surrounded by a wire fence and it had pillars and the pillars -- in between the pillars there was barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were guards, maybe at intervals of 50 metres. There was a guard who had a dog with him too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once you got inside the perimeter, did you see another fence?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside the camp, there was, I could -- so to speak, another camp. There were three stables in which livestock had been kept previously, cattle, and in these three stables in which the detainees were kept, these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. three stables were also surrounded by barbed wire, and I noticed that perhaps two or three metres from that fence, there was a warning. It said, "Mines." And I assumed that it was mined too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, once you arrived at the camp, did you go inside an office of some kind?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived at the camp, they first took us to a long building which was an official office. We sat down there. We were on one side and the officers, officers were on the other side. They introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The officers who were there, had you seen, or met any of them before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen the commander of the camp, Popovic. I had seen him in the command when we were arranging this visit, and I think that this dark-haired officer who was also in the command, I think he was there in Manjaca too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did Commander Popovic speak to you first of all?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Popovic spoke to us. He introduced himself officially. He said that he was the commander of the camp, that the camp was under the 1st Krajina Corps, and that the prisoners were prisoners of war, men who had participated in the resistance, men who had resisted and had been arrested, and he said, and this is something that he repeated, he said that he was treating them in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and he emphasised that, their fate would be -- that they would be going to other countries in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the time you say he told you that these people -- these men, had been resisters, was this after the attack on Kozarac had taken place? Your visit to the camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about where these men had come from, where they had been resisting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how many men there were at the camp roughly, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was said that there were 1.270 or 1.290 detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you went round the camp, as much as you were given permission, did he tell you anything about the condition of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dark-haired officer later said -- he spoke about the conditions, about the accommodation in the camp. He said that there was a medical clinic in the camp for the sick, that the detainees were organised in the camp, that they had certain senior inmates, and that there was a certain order, so to speak, which had to be respected. He said that they had food; he didn't say what kind of food or how much. And he also said that they would be taken to third countries, other countries, and he also said that we would visit the camp, and mentioned that we couldn't speak to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you allowed to go round the camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were allowed to go around the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you went round the camp, who was with you? I mean not -- to make it clear, from the military side.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dark-haired officer was with us. He was always with us. For sometime the commander, Commander Popovic was with us, or perhaps he was with us all the time. I can't remember exactly right now. I know the dark-haired officer was always with us. And there were perhaps another two or three men, officers, I don't know who they were, but in any event, I felt that each one of us had one officer, one soldier, with him. So there were four military men plus the dark-haired officer, and the commander was there, although he explained, as we were visiting the camp, he explained what there was in the various buildings in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the first area that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first went inside the building which we had entered, where that office was located in which we had been met, and inside that building we entered a room and they said it was a medical clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met two -- yes. We spoke to someone there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who did you speak to there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met two doctors, so to speak. I thought they were doctors. They were wearing white overcoats, doctors' overcoats and by their side was a military officer who was standing when we entered that room and they told us, "This is a medical clinic," and to the left there was a bed, medical bed, a hospital bed, and there was a cupboard, a medical cupboard for medicine and I noticed that it was empty. And we spoke to these people who were wearing these white overcoats. It was very revealing for me at that moment. I saw that these people in the white overcoats were afraid. And then after the conversation, and when I had a look below, I noticed that one of them was wearing shoes that had been torn. He was wearing big shoes that had been torn. I realised that they were, in fact, detainees. He introduced himself. Neither one of them was a doctor. But I think that they said that they were orderlies, medical orderlies, they weren't doctors. And they told us about the health situation in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In summary form, and I mean in summary, Mr. Dzonlic, what did they say were the medical problems in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told us straight away that they had a shortage of medicines and they emphasised that there were quite a number of diabetes patients, quite a number of people with high blood pressure, that they were short of bandages, that they were short of vitamins. They asked, if possible, could we supply them with vitamins. Then there were quite a number of people with intestinal problems, stomach problems. And they specifically asked if we could provide the necessary medicines. But the greatest problem was the problem of people suffering from diabetes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they mention anything about the age of the detainees and any problems that might arise from that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that there were some elderly people there too, though I could feel that they could not speak freely. They were not free to say whatever they wanted to say. They were in fear. I could see that they were trembling and one could see fear in their eyes. So they did not feel free to tell us everything that they wanted to tell us, at least that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said they asked for bandages. Did they explain why they needed bandages?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked why they needed them, as did Professor Bajric, why they needed bandages. Did he didn't give us an answer. I remember that I also asked, "When you have so many sick people, and only this one single bed in the clinic, and you're short of medicines?" Again they didn't give me an answer so my impression was that they didn't dare speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was anything said by either of these two orderlies or whatever they were, people in white jackets, about any injuries to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after you'd been to this, as it were, clinic-type place, did you then go to the place where the prisoners were being held?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we had finished this conversation, they said that we would now be going to see where the detainees or the prisoners were being held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you taken to a stable?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left this room where we had had this conversation, we turned right. There was an asphalt road and we covered about 50 metres. To our left was the internal camp surrounded with wire, in which there were these three large stables. Personally, at that point in time, it never occurred to me that people were inside those stables. Then they again opened a large gate for us. We passed by the first, second and third stable, and they told us that we would enter this third stable, the last one from the entrance, and they opened the door and we entered inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the first thing that hit you as you -- or that you noticed when you went into that stable?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was horrible. The first thought I had was I had felt all my life that Auschwitz that I had seen on television and pictures of, was reality, but after all, it's only shown on films, and then it was that I realised that this was reality, and the association I had was of Auschwitz. It was a large stable for livestock. In the middle of the stable was a concrete path running from the front to the end. To the right and the left of that concrete path was a -- an iron fence, and below those fences, to the right and to the left, were the detainees, who were lying there. I noticed that most of them were lying down. They were in a lying position. And next to the iron fence, further inside the stable, there were quite a number of them queueing up for something, one behind the other. And I wondered. I didn't know why they were standing there. And then I realised, when we reached the end of the queue, one of the prisoners had in front of him a container full of water, and he was shaving them all. And I remember that it was full of hairs from the shaving. I knew that we had been told that we should not communicate with the prisoners but one just couldn't do that. So we did talk to them as we passed by. And the officers saw this. And on a number of occasions, they cautioned us not to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment, please. Who told you that you were not to communicate with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dark-haired officer whom they addressed as captain. He said that we should not communicate with them. He had told us this in the office when he received us, and also while we were in the stable, he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cautioned us to that effect, not to talk and not to communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever discover what this officer's name was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said yesterday that I had my own diary where I noted down all the meetings, the times and the names of all those present, but I had to destroy them. I had all that recorded but unfortunately, I don't have it any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you, what were the prisoners wearing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it very strange. I came believing that these were prisoners of war, as they had insisted, but I noticed that these were people, ordinary civilians. No one was in uniform. They were all dressed -- there were some people in pyjamas, there were people who were bare foot. There were people with short-sleeved T-shirts but I didn't see a single one of the detainees wearing a uniform of any kind. And I found this very strange and I realised then that these were not prisoners of war. Perhaps they were because that was the status they were given and treated as such, but essentially they were civilians. And this was proven to be true during our communication with a certain number of prisoners. I asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before we move on to any communication, can we just finish the descriptions, please? You told us about the clothing. Did you notice anything about the condition of the men?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in a terrible condition. I remember one of them, I had the feeling that his eyes would pop out of his head, he was so skinny. And they were miserable looking. There were some with blood stains. They were beaten up. Most of them were lying down. They couldn't even stand or sit up. As we walked along the stable, one could hear moans by individuals. I remember one was standing immobile, as if he was dead and I asked, "What's wrong with him?" And somebody said, "His neck has been broken." I saw them covered in blood. They were in a dreadful, dreadful physical and mental state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they have any kind of bedding that you could see?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sleeping on the concrete and lying on the concrete, on which, but not throughout, there was straw. And over the straw, there was a blanket. But there wasn't straw everywhere so that there were some people who were lying directly on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The ages of the men, what sort of ages was the range? What sort of -- bad sentence. What was the range of ages that you saw?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some underage men and there were some very old men. So the range was between 15 and 70 or maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us you were able to speak to some of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't speak to them but we did speak to them nevertheless, and the dark-haired officer kept saying that we should stop talking to them that we were not allowed to speak to them but we paid no attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you were able to speak to them, what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I personally am concerned, I spoke to about five or six men. I asked them how they were, where they were from. One of them said that he was from Prijedor, that he had been taken in his own house, they came to my house and took me away, he said. Another one said he was also from Prijedor, that he had been taken, picked up from his garden, where he had been working. They came and took him away. He said that he had been brought from Omarska. One was from Bosanska Dubica. One said that he was from Derventa, that he had been brought there from the Stara Gradiska camp, where he had been detained, and that he had been brought to Manjaca. I asked each of them whether they had resisted, and all of the ones I spoke to said that none of them was in the resistance or a member of any armed force, but that they were civilians who had been rounded up in their houses and fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just pause there for a moment again, please? Firstly, you've mentioned Stara Gradiska. Do you know what Stara Gradiska was, what kind of camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, there was a prison there, a well-known prison. But as far as I know, it was also a camp, a prison and a camp, under the JNA, where they took prisoners to that camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just for the -- so that the Court understands, where is Stara Gradiska, is it in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stara Gradiska is not in Bosnia. It is in Croatia. As you cross the bridge separating Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia, the bridge over the Sava, once you cross the Sava, you enter Croatia and that is where the Stara Gradiska camp was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the smell like in that stable?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is impossible to describe. It's a smell that I never in my life had felt before. It's impossible to describe in words. But it indicated that these people had not had a bath since they had come there, that they had no running water to wash with or to bathe in. Secondly, they were lined up like sardines in a tin in an area of some -- an area that would be sufficient to house half the number of people in there. According to my estimate, there were about 350 to 400 men there. Secondly, because this used to be a stable, it was always a stable in the past for livestock, so you could smell the stench of manure and livestock and all this had mixed together so that the smell is simply indescribable. And it was very hard to breathe even inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any sanitary facilities?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw, when we had toured the stables, they showed us the other part of the camp, and I saw, in the immediate vicinity of those stables, a so-called field toilets lined up one to another. There were ten to 15 of them, made out of wooden boards. And the stench was dreadful coming from them, and then I asked this dark-haired officer what it was, and he said it was the toilets. The toilets were right next to where they were housed. And also in the immediate vicinity was the improvised kitchen where they had their meals so that the conditions were absolutely unhygienic and inappropriate for human beings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any shower facilities or bath facilities?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us that the kitchen was right next to the field lavatories. Was there any food that you saw at the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that this was their kitchen. However, it was about the same length as the stable with a roof over it, and along the whole length there were quite high boards so that the detainees couldn't sit and eat, they had to eat standing up. And some 30 metres from that covered area was a military vehicle which they described as a kitchen. It is a mobile military vehicle where the meals were cooked. And that's what they called the kitchen. Around this vehicle there were four or five men who were also prisoners, who, I assume, and we did communicate with them, they were the cooks, who prepared the food they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The question I'm sorry, Mr. Dzonlic, was did you see any food or was there any discussion about the food that was given to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see any food. And as for the cooks, we did talk to them about food, and they said that that is where the food was cooked, but they didn't tell us what kind of food. They just said that that is where the meals were prepared in this cauldron or whatever, but we didn't see any food. Nor did we have any discussions about food.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you visit all three stables during that time you were there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't visit all three stables. When we left this first stable, we entered the second stable, which was identical to the first. And we went through the same procedure. We came out and then this dark-haired officer said, "It's enough now. You'll go out now." And then we will bring ten prisoners from each of these buildings to talk to. I asked that we be allowed to enter this third stable, which was in fact the first you come to when you enter this closed area, but he said, "No, you can't go inside the third one. You'll go out of this internal encampment," and he would bring ten prisoners from each of the stables.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were a number of prisoners brought to where you were?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stood in front of the entrance, and we noticed that from each of the stables, most probably ten were coming out in a line, one behind the other, with their hands on their backs and their heads bowed, and they came up to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you recognise any of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I screamed out. I screamed out, I said, "There is my brother." And the Commander Popovic said to me, "These things also happen in life."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you been aware that your brother was being held in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know he was in Manjaca. But I knew, and I thought, that he was in Stara Gradiska because we had learnt that he was there. I didn't know that he was being held at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your brother's job at that stage in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother is a mechanical engineer, a designer, and he worked in a research and design centre in a company in Banja Luka called Jasinkar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When had you learnt that you -- you say you thought that he was in Stara Gradiska. How had you learned that he was in Stara Gradiska, and when?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother was arrested in Okucani because escorting a sick man, he was going to Sweden. Then both he and this man, who had dual citizenship, he had Yugoslav and Swedish citizenship, when they were captured, they were taken to Stara Gradiska. This man was released two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. days later and he came to our house and he told us that they had been arrested and taken to Stara Gradiska, that he had been released but that my brother was still in Stara Gradiska. This was, I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First, Okucani is where?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okucani is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was your brother at that stage involved in any kind of resistance?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My brother was a civilian and he was escorting this patient who had documents saying that he'd needed an escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally this before the break, how old was your brother at that time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother is two years older than me, so he was 34 then. He was born in 1957. And this happened in 1992. So he was 35.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break, resuming at 5 to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Ms. Korner, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, you told us about your brother's arrest and how you saw him at Manjaca. Were you able to speak to him when you saw him at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- did he tell you how long he'd been at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he told me that he had been taken there from Stara Gradiska about ten days before we arrived there, on that day, before we arrived in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what sort of condition was he in?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, I thought that he was psychologically very afraid. When he approached me, the first thing he said was, "They haven't beaten me." I didn't ask him about that but he told me that immediately. I always wondered why he told me that. I thought that perhaps he wanted to tell me that I shouldn't think about that. But later I found out that they beat him but this is something that he wanted to tell me. He didn't want me to worry and he said that they hadn't beaten him. He was quite afraid, and he was quite thin in comparison to the way he looked when he left. And that was about a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any conversation with any other detainees, prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the pause, I remembered that as we were passing through the stable, one of the detainees, one of the prisoners, told me that "There are other detainees, real prisoners of war, about 300 of them, and they are somewhere deep in the woods, in some houses, wooden huts. No one can approach them and you can't have access to them." And when these 30 detainees or rather ten from each stable, came to speak to us, we listened to what one gentleman had to say. He had crutches. One of his legs was broken and he was supporting himself on crutches and he said that his name was Filipovic, and that he was from Kljuc. He spoke and another gentleman who introduced himself as -- I can remember his surname, Bender, also spoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did Mr. Bender come from? Did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also came from Kljuc. They were both from Kljuc, gentlemen Filipovic and Mr. Bender.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when they spoke to you, were the officer that you described with the dark hair, was he there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were sitting by our sides. They were standing by our sides. And Commander Popovic then appeared because as far as I can remember, he didn't enter the stables with us, and when we came out of the stables to see the detainees, Commander Popovic also arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as best you can remember, what did Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Bender tell you about the conditions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Bender were very courageous, and they told me exactly what they had said and they said this in a very sincere way and they told us about everything that had been done to them in the camp. They talked about being starved. They said that they would receive a quarter of a slice of bread every day; that was a meal. And it was accompanied by some water. They said that they were maltreated every day and beaten every day, and that at night, it was the worst because they would call them and take them out of the stables. They would beat them until they were exhausted. He said that they would put them in pits of some kind and then jump on them. He said that there were quite a few people who were almost dead. I was really surprised by the courage that these people had, the courage they had to say these things and I thought it would be better if they didn't say such things because we could see for ourselves what condition the people were in. And I thought about what would happen to them, what would happen to these people, to Bender and to Filipovic because of what they had said, because of the fact that they had said exactly what had been done to them. And I would like to repeat this. I remember they said it was worst at night because they would call them and take them out to maltreat them and beat them, and they said that quite a few people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just stop there for a moment? Did they say how the beatings took place? In other words, with fists or with weapons or what?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that they used wooden sticks to beat them and they said that when they would beat you with copper cables, that was the worst sort of beating, and they said they did this to people whom they wanted to kill because it seems that this cable is so strong that men succumbed to their wounds. They would kick them too and put them in these pits in this beaten state and then they would jump on them. So, very often, some -- a certain number of people who had been taken out of the stables wouldn't come back. They were killed. He didn't mention the names of people. He just gave a precise description of the number of people that they beat and how they did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they say who was doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers on duty and the guards who were in the camp. He didn't give any names but he said they would come for them at night, they would call them, they would take them out, they were the guards and the people who were guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, to jump ahead just for a moment, you say that you were concerned about the fact that Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Bender were saying all this. Why were you concerned?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was concerned because they were saying this in such a public way, in front of these officers and camp commanders. They were talking about what had been done to them in a very public manner, and I thought that when we left they would do all sorts of things to them because they really told me what they had been doing to them. And the commander and the officers and all the military personnel allowed them to do this. They didn't interrupt them when they were speaking about this to us. I felt that something would happen to them, because of the sincerity with which they provided us with this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you later hear about the deaths of Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Bender?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about the deaths of both these men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Approximately how long after your visit did you hear that they were dead?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps ten or 15 days after that. I think it was perhaps ten or 15 days, but I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly, you've dealt with the fact that this visit took place after the attack on Kozarac and after you'd made a number of visits. Can you tell us what month it was that you made this visit?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was towards the end of May or perhaps it was the beginning of June. That was the period more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We may be able to get a date through a different route. After you had finished your visit, did you prepare a report of that visit?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we had finished this conversation with the detainees --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to -- I know there was more in the camp but I'm trying to get at the date, Mr. Dzonlic. That's why I'm going ahead slightly. Did you prepare a report when you'd finished your visit?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I prepared a report on the visit to the Manjaca camp, and I submitted it to the headquarters of the UNHCR, to Mrs. Ruby Ziebert and I submitted it to Mr. Beat at the International Red Cross. It was a signed report on the visit and on the conditions in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of your report, what did the International Red Cross do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We managed to arrange with the International Red Cross -- according to our first agreement, we arranged that the International Red Cross would enter the camp in -- within eight days' time but I think that perhaps 20 days passed before they managed to enter the camp, and so to speak, put all the detainees on record and take control of the -- of the camp. And I think that the situation in the camp was then a lot better than when we were there. They managed to become the patron, so to speak, of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So although you can't remember an exact date, your visit took place sometime after the attack on Kozarac and before the International Red Cross went to the camp for the first time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We were the first to enter the camp. A lot earlier than the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I went ahead there because I just wanted to try Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and establish a time frame. You've told us about your conversation with Mr. Bender and Mr. Filipovic. At the end of that conversation, did you return to the offices where you'd originally seen Commander Popovic and his officers?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We returned to the same office where we had been received when we arrived at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what did you say to the commander about what you'd seen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the commander that they were not acting in accordance with the Geneva Conventions in the camp and I remember that before I went to the camp I took a copy of the Geneva Conventions with me and I studied the rules and procedure of the Geneva Conventions, and I objected that there was not a public notice in the camp stating the rights of all the detainees. I objected to the living conditions in the camp. And I said that these conditions were not conditions fit for human beings. These were conditions fit for animals. I objected to the food, because on the basis of Bender's statement and on the basis whatever Filipovic said, I found out how much food they were being given. We asked them to allow us to provide supplies of medicine, because there were quite a few old people and sick people. I also asked, since the Commander Popovic was quite firm about the fact that the detainees would be going to other countries, I told the commander that I doubted -- I wasn't convinced by his position that they were prisoners of war, and to support my claim I said that I had seen my brother in the camp. I don't know the other people, I said, but I know my brother and I know that he wasn't a member of any kind of armed force. And on the basis of what people said, on the basis of statements made by people who said that they had been taken from their houses, from their gardens, it was possible to conclude that civilians were in question. He remained firm and said that they would be going to other countries, and I then suggested that all the detainees be placed under the patronage of UNPROFOR because at the moment they were suggesting the presence of the Canadian UNPROFOR that they make a basis near Banja Luka and that we place them in that basis and that they be under protection there. We didn't want them to go to other countries but he remained firm and he said that they could only go to other countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you said to him these men were not prisoners of war but civilians, did he respond to that at all? Other than saying what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all he said. He said these were prisoners of war. They will be going to other countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you tell him that you were going to make a report to the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that I would do it as soon as I returned, that I would submit a report to the International Red Cross on the state in the camp and that I would request that the International Red Cross enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you, please, to look very briefly at a video that you've had an opportunity to see before. I just want to ask you a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it was shown to Mr. Medic yesterday but I just want to ask him two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we pause the video for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, this is, as you can see, the inside of Manjaca. We've seen some prisoners there. It was taken in August of 1992. First of all, is that how you saw the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were they in this sitting position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't sitting. The ones I can see here, the ones who are sitting, when we entered, they were standing in a line, but those further down, they were lying down. They were all lying down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue playing it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please. Sorry, could we just run it back for a moment and pause at that shot? The shot of the inside of the stable, please? Thank you. Can we pause there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about the shoes? Is that how the shoes were? Or were people actually wearing the shoes?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were wearing them and the shoes weren't like this. And there weren't that many people on this concrete passage, as in this -- as in this image.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. Can we move on, then, for a moment, please? Sorry, can we move the film?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, pause please. Sorry. All right. We needn't go back. Yes, that man there, do you recognise him, the one with the glasses?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the commander of the camp, Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we pause, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us that the men were very thin. Were they as thin as or fatter or about the same? Some of them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were even thinner than the one in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just move on for a moment, play film?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or that gentleman? Did you see anybody that thin?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw people who were this thin, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been informed and I could be wrong, but I've been informed that this particular man that the Prosecution knows who he is, and knows that he was a person who was suffering from cancer and that his condition is not reflection of conditions in Manjaca but a reflection of the disease that he was suffering from. I think the Prosecution knows that. I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know where Mr. Ackerman has got that information from. I certainly don't know that. If Mr. Ackerman wants to supply me with the source of his information and the name of the man, we will certainly do a check.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The caption even says that these are people that came there only three days before from Omarska so his condition could have nothing to do, I would think, with Manjaca, in any event, and I'll try to run down the source of that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say I accept entirely a number of these prisoners had been transferred from Omarska. I'm not asking -- that's why I'm deliberately phrasing the question, "Did you see anybody as thin as this?" Sorry, could we have the film again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can just run it to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, on the film we've just seen, Mr. Dzonlic, were the numbers that you saw roughly the same as the numbers that we can see in that film, the numbers of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that. One could say that, that the numbers were something like that, but as I was saying, there weren't that many on the concrete passage way but there were more people lying down on the other side, but the numbers were something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finally on the topic of Manjaca, then, Mr. Dzonlic, whilst you were at the camp, did you make any requests as to the release of people?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We did make the request for release, for the release of certain categories of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What sort of categories did you ask for?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We noticed while visiting the camp that there were quite a number of men under age, quite a number of those who were ill, elderly people, we noticed that. But we asked the camp commander whether there were any religious officials and he said there were, and then we made the request that religious officials should be released, as well as the children who were underage, the elderly and the people who were seriously ill.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you made the request to the camp commander. Did he give you an answer then?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he said that this could be discussed and that it would be possible but he didn't say that he would release them. He said that we should make such a request in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he tell you to whom that request should be addressed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said we should address it to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, that we should take it there and hand it in, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you draft such a request?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did, on behalf of our office, we drafted a written request for such a release, and I think that, whether it was Fadil Medic or Professor Bajric, one of the two, took the request and handed it in to the command in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you don't know the answers, then say so, but you say it was a request addressed to the command. Was it addressed to anybody in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. command, a particular officer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know to whom personally it was addressed. I just know that we did draft such a request but to whom personally it was addressed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as a result of that request, were, in fact, a number of people released, some days later?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly how many people?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think around 100, 110, something like that, 120.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what sort of types of person were in that 120?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among them, as far as I can remember, there were about ten or 15 religious officials. Then maybe 20 or so minors. Then 30 or so men over 70. And the rest were seriously ill and beaten up people. There were some on stretchers even.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want now to move to a different topic, please, before I ask you to look at some of the documents that you've already looked at. You've told us about the two crisis staffs, the regional and the municipal Crisis Staff. The municipal assembly, did that meet at all during the period beginning of May and September? I'm sorry, take it back to July, July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly did meet but very rarely. But there were sessions. I would not be able to say exactly how many sessions the assembly held, but there were some.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At some stage, had your party, the SDA, made any decision with regard to attendance by members of your party at the assembly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We took the decision to withdraw from the assembly and we instructed our deputies to walk out of the assembly. This was done both by us and the HDZ party, which made a similar decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that decision or instruction, to your members not to attend, followed by everyone, that is to say, the members of your party?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
