utterances.text: As far as I'm able to recall now, I think that we had 13 deputies in the municipal assembly. Two deputies turned a deaf ear to our decision and did not observe it and stayed on in the assembly. One was a gentleman, by occupation a dentist. I think his surname was Busatlic and another deputy from the locality of Vrbanja I think his name was Handan. And the two of them did not observe our decision. Nor did the Vice-President of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly, Adem Gunic. The others did walk out of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The dentist, did he have any particular relationship with any member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- that Mr. Batar who was in the SDS, was his kum at his wedding, the best man at his wedding. Either Busatlic was his best man or Mr. Batar was Bustalic's best man. Anyway, one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see in Banja Luka, during the period of time before you left in 1993, a particular motor car, a red Kombi?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see a red vehicle, a red Kombi, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what sort of circumstances?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, I was passing by the building of the Glas daily newspaper in Banja Luka, which was right close to where I live, and this red van drove by. I think it was a Renault pickup truck and the rear doors were open. One could hear very loud Serbian music from the car, and inside there were about ten or so men in some sort of uniforms. They also held something that looked like baseball bats in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to see what sort of uniform it was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were olive-green but they were not like the regular uniforms worn by the Yugoslav People's Army, the regular troops, but they were of the same colour, but they were not exactly the type worn by all the regular troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the activities of this particular vehicle and occupants?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those men went around town intentionally to spread fear among citizens. They would suddenly appear in various restaurants or coffee bars, looking for particular individuals, and I heard that they would take people away, beat them, and I think their aim was to terrorise the citizens, because they moved around at a very slow pace, at 20 or 30 kilometres an hour, and they circled round town. They drove around town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you personally know anyone who was picked up by these men?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I know one man, whom they beat up, but they didn't take him away. They just beat him. They reached a pub near the Ferhadija Mosque and his name was Emir. They entered the bar and they beat him up but they didn't take him away. I know they beat him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about these men wearing as it were, irregular uniform. During this period, did you see irregular military forces? In other words, forces that did not appear to be part of the JNA or the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, in what circumstances did you see them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would frequently see, as I walked along the street in which I lived, but also from a window in my apartment, I would see three or four, and sometimes even ten or 15, buses go by full of soldiers who were dressed differently. They wore red caps on their heads, like berets, red berets, and they were passing by on their way to Jajce. I assume they were going towards the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll stop you. You were saying they were passing on their way to Jajce. What made you say that they were going to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that road leads to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And perhaps you can just explain to the court what during this period of time was happening at Jajce?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were intensified battles going on in Jajce and I remember that they were saying in Banja Luka that there was very strong resistance in Jajce and that they were afraid. I remember that they thought that because close by is the Bocaci hydro power plant and there was talk in town that they would lose Jajce and they were afraid that the regular army, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would gain control of the hydro power plant and release the water and the whole of Banja Luka would be flooded. However, after a short period of time, I know that one morning I woke up and the story in town was that Jajce had been liberated and thousands of trucks arrived, shooting around, these military trucks came, once they had managed to enter Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we all understand clearly, who had succeeded -- sorry, who had liberated Jajce?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs said that they had liberated Jajce. That is what they said when they entered Jajce. They said they had liberated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Jajce was being resisted or the entry into Jajce was being resisted by whom? Which army or which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosniaks and the Croats were putting up joint resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've described these buses going through with men who were wearing red berets. Did you ever see any of these irregular forces at a closer range?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see them in town, in groups of three members, who were dressed -- all dressed up, as we would say in Banja Luka. They wore high leather boots up to their knees, short leather jackets with fur collars, Ray-ban glasses and fur caps with a cockade on it. And they were all of more or less equal height, over 1 metre 90 centimetres and they marched around town. And the story in town was that these were Seselj's forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you ever given an opportunity to hear any of these men, these type of men, paramilitary forces, talking?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, in a pizzeria, which was in the centre of town close to the well known Kusma Banja Luka bar, a pizzeria had been opened, and on one occasion, we were sitting in the garden of that pizzeria, and ten or so men arrived, who were wearing black uniforms. We called them Ninja; that is how they were dressed. And they spoke in the Ekavica dialect. They had a lot of money on them. And they said that they had brought Serb money from Belgrade in transport vehicles. And he said that in future this would be our money which would be used in Banja Luka. A part of that money, they said, would be left here and a part of it would be taken to Knin, the Knin Krajina. They stayed there for maybe three or four days, and I would see them every night, they would come every evening. They would act extravagantly. They would buy drinks for everyone with that money.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pausing there for a moment, you said they spoke with the Ekavica dialect. Where is that from?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They spoke Ekavica. It is the original Serbian dialect. The people in Belgrade use it. I was -- I served in Belgrade. I did my military service there, and I'm familiar with the Belgrade dialect. And they said so themselves. They said they had come from Belgrade and that they had brought cash, which would be the currency in Banja Luka, and that a part of it would be taken to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the Serbian money that they brought with them, did that circulate in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from then on, we started paying in Serbian money. It became the regular currency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, one final matter: During this period of time, between May, 1992, roughly, and February, 1993, when you left, did non-Serbs leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what sort of numbers?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Departure from Banja Luka was very clearly established and planned by the Serb authorities, which thereby ethnically cleansed and moved out more than 50.000 Bosniaks and close to 30.000 Croats. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment, please. First of all, the 50.000 Bosniaks and close to 30.000 Croats, are you saying all of those left in the period before you left Banja Luka in February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not before I left, but I'm saying the total number that left, at the end, but while I was there, people were leaving. There were so-called convoys arranged through agencies held by Perka, but it was known as Brdjanin's agency in town. And there was a very clear-cut procedure for this exodus and removal. There were three directions. One was in the direction of Travnik. And there were convoys going there twice a week, on Tuesday and Wednesdays. And then another direction was towards Croatia via Okucani and Novska, and a third using the corridor towards Serbia. But the one towards Travnik and central Bosnia was limited to younger people, the elderly and women, and very rarely men of military age could go towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you pause for a moment, please, Mr. Dzonlic, because I just want to ask some questions. First of all, you said that the convoys were arranged through agencies held by Perka. Who or what was Perka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Perka headed the agency. The official name of the agency was the agency for resettlement. And you addressed it after a complicated procedure which preceded this for you to be able to receive a document allowing you to move out. I don't know who this Perka was, this lady, but I know she headed the resettlement agency and its offices were in Mala Carsija opposite the bridge in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that this agency was known in the town as "Brdjanin's agency." Why was that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone in town said that this was Brdjanin's agency, and that is how people -- everyone called it, Brdjanin's agency. Some people even thought that Brdjanin and Perka were related. But they referred to the agency as Brdjanin's and later on, I learnt that the Krajina Crisis Staff had taken a decision to set up this agency for resettlement and as Brdjanin headed that Crisis Staff, it was probably for that reason that it was known as Brdjanin's resettlement agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the -- this was something that was orchestrated -- I'm sorry, I think I need to run this back just to find the exact words. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just want to make sure that I don't get the wrong words. Yes. You said that the departure from Banja Luka was clearly established and orchestrated by the authorities. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know that the authorities arranged it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that you knew that the authorities arranged it. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the procedure for departure, for leaving Banja Luka, involved the bodies of the authorities in Banja Luka municipality and certain public institutions, and you were obliged to contact them to get permission for leaving. First, you had to go to the police, the centre for public security, or the police, and say that you were leaving and make up an address that -- where you were going. So people would write down that they were going to Sweden, to Czechoslovakia, to Greece, to Germany. After that, you would go to the National Defence Secretariat, which would take your military documents from you. You would have to hand in your uniform if you had been a mobilised conscript or if you had a military assignment after doing your military service in the former JNA. Once you managed to do that, you had to go to the court to get a certificate that there were no criminal proceedings against you. Once you got that document, you would go to public institutions such as the post office, the power distribution centre, the heating facility. You would have to get a certificate saying you were not a telephone subscriber or if you were a telephone subscriber that you had paid all your bills. And also to the power distribution organisation, to make sure you had paid your electricity bills and your heating bills. Then you had to go to the municipal assembly, to the tax office, to receive a certificate that you owe no tax. Then you would have to go to the cadaster of the Banja Luka municipality attached to the courts to show that you don't have any real estate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to stop you for a moment. I think before we go any further, was this something that always happened? In other words, before these events in 1992, or was this something that had only happened as a result of the Crisis Staff and the like?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the result of decisions of the Crisis Staff. Before that, it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't have to go and go round all these bodies, as it were, obtaining certificates until the Crisis Staff came into existence?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, I interrupted you. What else did you have to do before you leave? You said you had go to the cadaster of the Banja Luka municipality to show no real estate. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to go to the cadaster of Banja Luka municipality to make sure that you had fulfilled all your obligations, that you had paid your property tax, tax on any property you owned, and as far as I remember, I collected 15 different documents from various bodies and public institutions. Of course, each of those had to be paid for, the price being 20 to 30 German marks on an average for each. And what would happen then, once you had been issued all these certificates by these various institutions, would you have to go to a kind of office behind the Bosna Hotel to make a statement that you were voluntarily and for economic reasons leaving Banja Luka. At one point in time, you even had to pay into the Defence Ministry account 250 or 350 German marks, I can't say exactly. I remember that at a meeting of the executive board of the SDA, we resisted and opposed this and we informed the UNHCR, which reacted and about a month later, this decision was cancelled, requiring people to pay in 250 or 350 German marks for the Defence Ministry. Then you had to apply to an office opposite the city bridge and you would have to hand to them all these certificates you had collected and you'd have to pay 50 German marks to them - that was the amount I had to pay - for them to give you a document which was called "permission for resettlement." But even that was not the end of the story. After that, you would have to go to this resettlement agency headed by Perka and you would have to pay there 100 German marks for her to put you on the list for removal, and Perka would give the list of names for people who had applied for resettlement to the police for control. The police would check it, return it to Perka. And then as I have already said, through the established corridors, you would leave, either towards Croatia, those who had letters of guarantees and the necessary documentation, or to Travnik or the corridor towards Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in such an organised and planned manner, we estimated that every Tuesday and Wednesday, if there were only two busloads leaving, that would be 100 people, and four times a week, that would be 500 people times 12 months, so it's close to 5.000 a year, just in one direction. And there were three different directions or corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, just two further questions on this issue. First, you told us that you had to make a statement that you were voluntarily and for economic reasons leaving Banja Luka. Before you left in 1993, did you have friends and acquaintances who left?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For what reason were they leaving?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason for their departure was fear. That was the main reason. People were very scared. It wasn't for economic reasons. The Bosniaks in Banja Luka were rich. They were affluent. But the main reason was fear. And secondly, they had lost their jobs. They had lost their flats, their accommodation, and this made people leave. This is why they felt they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were people allowed to take with them their savings, for example, money in the bank account or any other moveable property?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't. There was a restriction. People could leave with no more than 300 German marks. That's the amount you could take out with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about items such as silver or anything that they had collected of that nature?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People hid these items in various ways. They would sew them into their coats. They would hide them this bags, hide them in their jackets. They would put these items into creams. They would open a pot of cream, women's cream. They would put their gold and jewellery in there, their diamond rings in there and they would close these pots of creams as if it were just women's cosmetics. No one was able to wear these items, this jewellery, publicly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the buses containing these emigrants left, were any searches carried out by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I know that when I left, there were no searches, when we entered the buses. But when the other buses left, I don't -- that didn't happen, I don't think, but I heard that there were searches in Bosanska Gradiska. There was a checkpoint there and I later heard from people who managed to get through that they had stripped them and searched them and looked through their bags and through their affairs. But at the place from which they left, there were no searches.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally on this topic, did you ever see persons in Banja Luka passing through from other areas of Bosnia to Travnik or any of the other places you've mentioned? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't but I heard about such cases. I heard that a few convoys from Prijedor and Bosanski Novi had passed through Banja Luka in the direction of Travnik and I remember that one of these convoys fared very badly at the Korincanski Stijene near Travnik. They came from the direction of Prijedor and went through Banja Luka and they were killed over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry about that. We are going to hear other evidence about that. Thank you, Mr. Dzonlic. Then finally, on the topic of conditions in Banja Luka, during the period whilst you were still in Banja Luka, did you actually see any damage done to any mosque?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the mosque near my place of residence, the mosque which we called Potpecinska and which I referred to at the beginning of my statement. I referred to this mosque at the beginning of my statement. It was the first one to be set on fire. And I with the late Banja Luka mufti, went there personally, went to this mosque. It had been damaged. Part of the roof had collapsed. And the entrance had been broken, and some of it had burnt. We arrived there at the scene on the following day after this had happened. That's one case. The other case that I saw, and at which I was present, was in the premises of the Islamic Community, which is very near the Ferhadija Mosque, and this happened when, as they said, they released, in inverted commas, Jajce. The army entered Banja Luka. There were columns. They came with lorries. Rifle-launched grenade hit the base of the mosque, which was between the building of the Islamic Association and the Ferhadija Mosque, these two buildings which are very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say you were present. Do you mean you saw this actually happen, the grenade hit the base?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it. But the grenade didn't explode. It was shot from a lorry which was circling the mosque. It was fired but it didn't explode. We then came out of the premises of the Islamic Community and that's when we saw this grenade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The mosque that you did see that had been set on fire, could you see, when you examined it, you say you went the following day, how that fire had been caused? In other words, was it by an explosion or clearly somebody just setting it on fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I doubt that this person is an expert on determining cause of fires and things of that nature. If he is, let him be qualified as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Generally speaking, he might give us the necessary information, Mr. Ackerman. He doesn't need to be a qualified explosives expert to answer that question. I mean, we could -- we could see an explosion outside and fire following immediately after. None of us are experts and we would be able to say that the fire that we saw was -- followed immediately an explosion. So let him answer the question. I don't think I find any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you hear, Mr. Dzonlic, about this mosque?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard, or rather I heard, that the Potpecinska Mosque had been set on fire. I received such information in the premises of the Islamic Community. It was said that on the previous day, the previous night, in the evening, it was said that the Potpecinska Mosque had been set on fire. We immediately went to the mosque. I don't know whether it had been hit by a grenade. I don't know how it was set on fire. I really couldn't comment on this. But I entered and part of the mosque's roof had collapsed, the entrance -- the door, the wooden door, had burnt down, and part of the ceiling as you entered the mosque, this part which was also wooden, had collapsed and I know that the mufti was very sad about this. It was the first mosque that had been touched, so to speak, and damaged in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you asked last week sometime to have look at a video?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I emphasise this was a video made in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To see if you could identify the mosque that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was requested, and I identified the mosque which I'm now referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a short clip and just see if you can tell us, A, is this the mosque, and, B, whether the damage that you noticed was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Dzonlic, when you see the mosque? I hope it's in the right place. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's mosque but it wasn't in this state when I -- when I went there, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pause the film for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see that it's virtually completely demolished. How much of this sort of damage had already been done? I mean what was standing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the mosque had all its walls intact. Only part of the roof, perhaps the right side, when you enter the mosque, the right side of the roof, half of the roof, had collapsed. It had fallen down. And all the surrounding walls were intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this image, they are completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So before you left Banja Luka in 1993, in February of 1993, the damage wasn't as great as this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's fine. I want to move now to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move to some documents. Your Honours, I don't know whether this would be perhaps an appropriate place to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it might. I want to double check that I've got the numbers right as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will reconvene --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we will break now and we will reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Will that be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly. It just seems to be a convenient place to check the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be our break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first document that I'm going to look at is, I've checked this time, it's right, it's been numbered P202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Its disclosure number was 416 and it's in volume 2 of the Banja Luka documents in my copy under divider 26, the second set of dividers, 26. Your Honour, may I say straight away most of these are documents that the witness hasn't seen before but what I'm doing is going to ask him about entries and say what knowledge he has of certain events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I'm now going to ask you to have a look again at some of the documents you looked at when you made your second statement to the investigator. Could you be handed, please, the B/C/S version so the number is P202B, I think. Now, before you were shown investigator, I think it's right you had not seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, if you go to the last page, it's signed by Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know who Stojan Zupljanin was at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was chief of the Security Services Centre based in Banja Luka, and I also knew that he was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware at any stage that he was a member of the Regional ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 23, which we can see on the fourth page, you will see an instruction, "In all our activities we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region." From your knowledge, as you described to us, of how a crisis staff would operate, were you surprised to see that the police were saying they had to obey procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not surprised. I was not surprised when I saw that the police has to observe the decisions of the Crisis Staff, because it is my opinion, and also on the basis of documents which I had and which I was able to see, at the top of the pyramid of power was the staff of the Autonomous Region and all bodies had to execute the decisions of the Crisis Staff, and to report back on tasks carried out and conclusions implemented further to instructions from the Crisis Staff. And I know that they placed themselves above the official organs of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by "the official organs of authority," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to the various secretariats within the municipality such as the Secretariat for National Defence, for the economy, the police, the assembly of the municipality, the executive council of the municipality. I'm thinking of those bodies of authority. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come to the executive council at a later stage. The second part of that paragraph refers to a deadline for weapons surrender on May the 11th, 1992. Do you remember anything about a deadline for the surrender of weapons in May?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I cannot remember this particular date, but I do know that there were certain deadlines regarding the surrender of weapons by whoever had any and I know that this deadline was extended on a number of occasions, so that it was never a fixed deadline. After that deadline, there were additional ones, that is the time limit was prolonged for the surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Serbs that you knew held weapons?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, almost all Serbs had weapons, almost all Serb that is I knew had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know of your own knowledge whether any of them surrendered their weapons?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that any one of them surrendered their weapons, and this proclamation on the surrender of weapons applied -- or rather it was responded to only by non-Serbs, those that had weapons. I don't know that any one of the Serbs returned their weapons, and it would be illogical for me, because they were armed. They had been armed about six months prior to this, throughout that period running up to this, they had been armed. So it would be illogical for them to hand back those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you know that the Serbs in the six-month period had been armed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just six months, but I know that they applied to the local communities within the municipality to take military uniforms, those that didn't -- hadn't had them issued to them and that weapons were being issued. And there was public talk about the Serbs being armed. It was general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from public talk or general knowledge, did you hear about this from anyone who was directly involved?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that my colleagues who were Serbs by ethnicity were issued uniforms and weapons. Behind the building where I lived, there were such a centre close to the students' hostel, where they went to pick up weapons and military equipment, and we Bosniaks would go to the same place to hand in our military equipment to that same centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you yourself have any weapons or military equipment?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have military equipment; that is, the bottom part of the uniform. I was never issued a weapon. And this military uniform, which was kept in a military bag, my father took it to this Rada Brnjesevic centre on my behalf and was given a certificate, certifying that I had returned the uniform. And I never had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't own a hunting rifle or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before I move to the last part of this document, can I ask, does Your Honours' copies -- do Your Honours' copies have any markings by those two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, if at the end of the session you hand them -- we copied them by mistake from somebody else's markings. There are clean copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now there are additional markings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't give it to you because there are additional markings that I have made now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask Your Honours then to note that the originals do not have these markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They can be substituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I know what the markings are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two exclamation marks. Next to paragraph 23 there is an exclamation mark and the following paragraph has another exclamation mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By giving evidence, which I know Mr. Ackerman hates, can I say that was done by somebody in the office reading the documents. It's not on the originals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally on this document, Mr. Dzonlic, could we go to the very last paragraph just before the signature which is marked "AD3"? Where Mr. Zupljanin was telling the centre council that a special countersabotage and counterterrorist police unit of about 150 was to be deployed in the regions in the most complex security operations, explains where -- what the makeup of this unit will be, and then says, "Its founding will be celebrated in Banja Luka at a special ceremony." Now, do you remember anything about any kind of ceremony like this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when the ceremony took place to celebrate the formation of special police forces in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you present when this ceremony took place?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in town, in the centre of town, next to the cultural centre, at the crossroads where the cultural centre and the Bosna Hotel are situated and quite a number of citizens came out into the streets to greet the participants and then special police forces paraded in town. I remember that vehicles passed by, equipment. We noticed, not just myself but other people who were present in the streets, there was even laughter because it was clear that these were really military vehicles that had just been painted over into blue, the police colour, but the painting wasn't done well, so one could see that these were military vehicles. I, for instance, recognised the military vehicle called Pinzgauer. The police never owned any such vehicle. Then also vehicles that resembled tanks. But the greyish-green colour could be seen of these vehicles so that people were laughing, saying, "All this is military property. It's just been painted over blue." I remember that some vehicles on the outside had black plastic or rubber covers over the vehicles. I also know that helicopters were flying over and they claimed that these were all the materiel belonging to the police. But due to what I've just said, it is my firm conviction that this was all military materiel that had just been camouflaged and painted over to appear to be police materiel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about the members of this special squad? Did they have any special uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a variety of uniforms. They were not like the police uniforms worn by policemen in the streets. There were camouflage, bluish-grey uniforms, plain blue uniforms, but they differed from the uniforms worn by the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see over the next -- I'm sorry, can I go back for a moment? This document is dated the 21st of May -- no, well there is a handwritten note so -- it's the 20th -- I'm so sorry, I'll start again. This meeting was held on the 6th of May and the special display was on the 12th of May. Did you see the members of this squad in Banja Luka after May?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we could leave that document, please, and move to the next series, Your Honours, which are the official gazettes of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The number is P227, disclosure number 3.69. I'm again going to ask that the witness be given the version in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, again, Mr. Dzonlic, did you ever see this Official Gazette in any publication in 1992 itself?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see this. I think I saw this document, or rather -- maybe not the entire document. But a part of the document. I didn't see it in this form, in the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the document you spoke about yesterday, that is to say one of the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Official Gazettes, who gets copies of the Official Gazettes?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Copies of Official Gazettes were distributed to all beneficiaries of budgetary resources, to economic entities, and other public institutions, establishments, schools, the PTT, the companies that were under state control.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were they ever published in newspapers or any other media?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not published in the daily newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that first decision that we can see, the actual gazette was issued in Banja Luka on the 5th of June of 1992, but if you turn over -- just checking --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just checking to see whether the B/C/S version is like ours and turns over the page or whether it's on the same -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first decision is dated the 4th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 1, it's an order for general public mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the order that you were talking about yesterday when you explained about what had happened to people who failed to respond?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's signed by a Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic, secretary of the National Defence Secretariat. Did you know Lieutenant Colonel Sajic or anything about him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him, but I had heard his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As what?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the context but I know that I had heard the surname and first name mentioned, Milorad Sajic. And I know it had to do with the military, but specifically, I don't know how I heard it or where I heard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it, but it's a familiar name to me and it had something to do with the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move to the second decision in this gazette, dated the following day, the 5th of May, which is a decision on the formation of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina signed by the president of the executive council, Nikola Erceg. Did you know Nikola Erceg?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know Nikola Erceg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my neighbour. He lived two floors below me, and he also worked in the company in which my father and brother worked in Jelsingrad and I knew him as a neighbour because we would see one another virtually on a daily basis as we came to and from home. So he lived two floors below me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's signed in a function as president of the executive council. Could you just explain to the Court what was the executive council?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the executive council of the Crisis Staff was, conditionally speaking, the government of the Crisis Staff. The operative body of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the existence of the Crisis Staff, did the executive council exist?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the structure of authority, there was the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka municipality and there was the executive council of the municipal assembly or the government of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the executive council, you say, was the operative body of the Crisis Staff, and before that, do we take it the operative body, then of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before it existed, and at this time, too, there was an executive council of the municipality of Banja Luka and of every other municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say "operative," what did it actually do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operative body is a body which implements conclusions and decisions of another body, in this particular case, the Crisis Staff. It also supervises, implements, monitors, and reports the crisis -- reports to the Crisis Staff on the implementation of assigned tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would it have any authority to act on its own? In other words, without a decision either by the assembly or in this case, the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It could not act independently. It executes the tasks assigned to it by the Crisis Staff and that is why it is responsible to the Crisis Staff for the execution and implementation of all conclusions. It cannot act independently without the approval and a decision by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would it have any kind of delegated authority? In other words, to make decisions within a certain limited sphere?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, it could take decisions for operational reasons. Sometimes the Crisis Staff may not be able to meet, a large number of people making up the Crisis Staff could not perhaps be convened and then it is envisaged that this operative body, in extraordinary circumstances, when something is urgent, may meet and take a decision. But subsequently the approval of the Crisis Staff would have to be required. And I think this executive council was formed for that precise reason, to be more efficient and operational. I don't know how many members sat on the council but probably fewer than on the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, finally, on the question of Mr. Erceg, did you ever go and speak to him about anything that you had seen in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to see him when I saw at the railway station in Banja Luka seven carriages for livestock full of people. And after learning about these facts, I went to the railway station and I saw those carriages, and I saw people with their hands stretched out from those carriages. I know it was hot. It was summertime. There were two women on behalf of Merhamet as well, and we tried to approach those people and we asked to bring them food and water. However, the military and the police were present and they wouldn't allow us to approach them. And one of the policemen said that we should, if we wanted to do anything for these people, that we had to address Nikola Erceg. So I went directly to see Nikola Erceg in the municipality building, which is across the road from the cultural centre, and Nikola Erceg had his office there on the second or the third floor, and I asked to be received by him, and he did receive me, and I told him about these people, and asked that Merhamet be allowed to give those people food. However, he answered that those people were in transit and that he was not competent for those people and that those people would be going to Doboj. We learnt -- I didn't see or hear, but I heard that 11 people had died, and I said that one day somebody would have to be held accountable for this. But he said that they could do nothing about it because those people were just passing. And that was the contact I had with Nikola Erceg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you told him that 11 people had died?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just look at the list that is printed there? And just let me ask you about some of the people on it. You told us about Brdjanin, Sajic you'd heard the name of, Kupresanin, Vojo Kupresanin, did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him but I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what context can you remember had you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had something to do with the police, as far as I'm able to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Erceg you've told us about. Radic you've told us about as well. Dr. Radislav Vukic, is that the man you were talking about yesterday who made the speech about the people in the hospital, Muslims in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He is the one. I think he was president of the Banja Luka SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Milovan Milanovic, did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard of him, and he had a holiday home on the seaside close to the holiday home my father had near the town of Sibanik. I know what he looks like but I never had any personal contact with him. He was a member of the SDS and he was working at the clinical centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that different -- is that the same place that Dr. Vukic worked, or different?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same clinical centre, but there were departments for anaesthesia, internal medicine, gynaecology and so on but it's the same institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us of your dealings with General Talic. Apart from that meeting that you've described to us, did you ever have any other meetings with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, when I was going to the command, to see about the permit, to see whether they had granted us authorisation to go to Manjaca, I saw General Talic, but we didn't have any contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Major Jokic, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin you've told us about. Now, the next name --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I make the point -- we are going to get a new translation done, but the name as translated is -- or as written in English is Dr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, can you tell us, please, what name is written in the B/C/S version by the number 11?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Dragolub Mirjanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not at all clear how that happened. This went in for translation and it was only picked up by Mr. Dzonlic when he saw this document the other day, but we will have to send it back for a correction. But the name should read Dr. Dragolub Mirjanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, the next name, Mr. Puvacic who was he?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was maybe a Prosecutor or perhaps a judge at the higher court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovo Rosic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also worked in the judiciary. He was also either a Judge or a Prosecutor. I know this about them but I can't say whether he was a Judge or a Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dubocanin, did you know him or Mr. Stevandic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or the last two names on the list, Bulic and Kesic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about either of them, apart from the last one, when I saw one document, Nedeljko Kesic was either the chief of state security, as they called it, but I didn't know that, the surname Kesic is one that is familiar to me in Banja Luka. I don't know him. But I subsequently found out from documents that he was the chief of state security in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next, can we move to the decision number 4? That's the fourth decision dated or headed at its meeting of the 8th of May. Now, item number 5 states that, "It is hereby requested that the military territorial authorities of the JNA start activities immediately in order to save the Serbian people in the areas along the most threatened front lines, Bosanski Brod to Derventa and Kupres to Glamoc to Bosansko Grahovo from genocide." What does that conclusion suggest to you, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it speaks for itself. It's clear what it says and I don't think we need to be favoured with his interpretation of it. It's clear on its face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I still want to hear the -- Ms. Korner finish her question because -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, can you throw any light on the events which led to this particular conclusion? If that satisfies Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, and this can also be seen from this conclusion, I know that at the front lines, where there was fighting, from Bosanski Brod to Derventa, at the time the Serbian forces had suffered heavy casualties in the surroundings of Derventa. I remember that they said that there was heavy fighting around Plehan, that's what they called the area, as far as I know. There was a Catholic monastery and a church there. Given that they had suffered heavy casualties and that they were unable to break through the line in these areas and the main objective of breaking through that line was to break through the corridor in the direction towards Belgrade, they would say, "If only we break through in Plehan, we will then take the corridor and everything shall be solved." And for these reasons, they adopted such a conclusion and asked the organs of the JNA to assist them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the Bosnian Serb forces that had suffered losses were separate, were they, from the JNA that's being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can move, then, please, to the -- I'm sorry, can we just for one moment stay on that document? Item number 7, says, "In the future, tickets for flights to --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a slight problem concerning the interpretation in response to the question as to whether the forces which assisted this offensive were JNA forces, or whether they were the same forces from Republika Srpska, the witness's response to this question was yes, and the interpretation I heard, according to the interpretation, the reply I heard was no. I would simply like to know whether the response to this question is yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I think, and if the witness has understood, as I would expect him to have, the observation made by Maitre de Roux, I think he's in a position to clarify it to us without the need for Ms. Korner to put the question again. Have you understood what Mr. de Roux stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have understood the question and I said yes to the Prosecutor's question. I said that the forces were separate. The Serbian forces were separate from the forces of the JNA, and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I have in my -- on my monitor, any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps we just better expand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb forces who had suffered these losses, where were they drawn from?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These forces came from -- we called them the Serbian forces. We called them paramilitary forces. They came from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from various towns and mostly from parts of Bosnian Krajina, and also these paramilitary forces, these so-called paramilitary forces, these forces were irregular ones from Serbia, as I said, and I said that I saw them in Banja Luka, members of Seselj's group and of Arkan's group, and there were forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and, for us, they were aggressive forces, forces of occupation. Because from the date of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we thought that all other forces that weren't under the control of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right, I think you've explained. So as far as you were aware, and I should ask you, where were you getting this information from?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what we saw in the field, there were forces which had come from Serbia, and secondly, for us, the legal organs of the independent and -- independent state of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had been recognised, the legal forces, were the only legal organs of authority, and we thought that all military and police forces, which were under the control of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after its independence had been recognised, we thought that such forces were regular ones and that all other forces were paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, perhaps I can just conclude this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you know, however, which forces outside the regular JNA were engaged in this, at that stage, losing struggle? In other words, did you get it from the media or from people who were there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the media, I found out that they were Serbian forces, that Serbian forces were at certain front lines, because there were reports that Serbian units were at the front lines of -- from Bosanski Brod to Derventa. They didn't mention paramilitary forces in the media. The paramilitary forces from Serbia were not mentioned but this was known. This was, so to speak, a public secret. In the town we would see certain members of paramilitary forces and they did not resemble units of the Serbian army, and we knew that they had come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like you to remind the witness before he leaves that he is not to discuss his testimony with anyone outside this Chamber at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say there are no other witnesses here at the moment, but it may be just as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzonlic, have you heard what Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Korner have just stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is one of the Rules of this Tribunal, and you will be violating a very important Rule should you communicate with others in relation, regarding -- regarding matters that you are giving testimony upon. So I take it that you will not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of my duties and thank you for the warning, as to my duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also knows, is aware, that you are a lawyer and that for sometime you were also a judge so fully understands your commitment. Thank you. We will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. In the meantime, if you can come forward tomorrow morning first thing with some kind of a time schedule for the rest of the next two months, the end of June possibly, or end of July, before we reach the summer recess, I think that would be very useful so that we can plan ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have completed it. I've given a copy to Ms. Korner. Ms. Fauveau has approved it. It's essentially complete. I know Ms. Korner agrees with part of it, probably not all of it. If you'd like, I can hand it to you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you discussed it with Maitre Pitron as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. Mr. Pitron I can't find. I don't know where he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maitre de Roux is behind and he took the joke. We will reconvene tomorrow morning and we'll possibly discuss these few remaining items.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've had a quick look and I'll go through it this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday the 28th day of February, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
